headline: Southside Monomoy: Albies on Top, Wahoo Underneath — Still
subhead: Terns are stacked over Monomoy's edge and something a lot bluer than a false albacore is cutting through the bait ball beneath them.
body_markdown:
There's a tern wheel that's been holding over the southeast corner of Monomoy for four straight days now, tight and low, dropping on peanut bunker getting pushed up from underneath. From a distance it looks like a standard albie push — and it is, there are albies stacked under those birds — but guys running out of Chatham and Stage Harbor have been watching bigger, faster flashes cut through the same bait, silver-blue and gone before you can call it. That's the wahoo. Same fish that's been showing off Southside Monomoy for two weeks now, and mahi mixed in with it, which is about as far from a normal late-September Nantucket Sound morning as it gets. We flagged this pattern last week — said if the warm water held, the wahoo bite wouldn't be a one-off — and here we are, still talking about it heading into the fourth week of fall.

The water's the reason. There's a warm tongue that's refused to break down, and it's parked itself right where the Sound spills out around Monomoy and down toward the Point Rip. That warm filament is also why the albies and bonito showed early and haven't left — bait's staying comfortable in water that should be cooling by now, and the predators are following it. Kings Point over on the Sound's western edge is still reading close to 71, and while that's a different piece of water than what's happening off Chatham, it tells the same story — this whole system is running warm for the calendar.

Great Point is fishing the way it should this time of year, which is to say inconsistent but worth the run when it clicks. The rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been the window — bonito mixed with albies crashing bay anchovies and small silversides, with the bonito running a little deeper in the water column than the albies, which stay up top smashing visible bait. Half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Hogy epoxy jig in bone or pink-white has been the call for both, worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. If the surface bite goes quiet, don't leave — drop a Deceiver or a small Game Changer down ten to fifteen feet on a sink-and-sweep and the bonito especially will still eat.

Sankaty's been a striper spot more than an albie spot this week. Bass in the 24 to 34-inch range are working the rip there on the bottom stages of the tide, taking peanut bunker imitations — 3-inch white RonZ or a 5-inch white Slug-Go — fished slow along the current seam where the clean water meets the roiled edge. Bluefish have been mixed in too, and they've been the more reliable player honestly, chopping bunker pods that are starting to stage up for the fall push. Bigger tides from this week's Harvest Moon are pulling more water than usual through the rip systems, which is speeding up bait movement and tightening the feeding windows — when it turns on, it turns on hard for 45 minutes to an hour, then goes dead until the next stage change.

Monomoy itself remains the most interesting piece of the whole Sound right now. Southside, in that stretch between the elbow and the rip off the point, boats are finding albies and bonito on top, striped bass working the same bait from below, sea bass and fluke still holding on the sandy bottom in 20 to 35 feet, and then whatever that wahoo and mahi show is turning into underneath all of it. Nobody's targeting the wahoo — there's no real tackle plan for it in Nantucket Sound, it's just showing up in the middle of everything else — but rods rigged for albies with 20-pound fluoro leader have gotten bit and broken off more than once out there this week, which tells you something about size and speed.

Fluke fishing has actually held up better than it usually does this late in September, another symptom of the warm water keeping fish shallower and more active than the calendar suggests. Horseshoe Shoal and the sandy stretches off Monomoy are still giving up keepers on Gulp swimming mullet in white or pink shad, tipped bucktails working the bottom on the last of the outgoing.

Looking ahead, the Harvest Moon tides should keep sharpening the feeding windows through the weekend — bigger water movement means bait gets funneled harder through the rips, which usually means shorter, more violent bites rather than long steady ones. If the warm filament holds through early October, expect the albie and bonito activity to keep building rather than fade, and don't be shocked if the wahoo talk out of Southside Monomoy keeps going too. The thing to watch is any real cold front — the first one that actually knocks water temps down will start pushing this whole system south fast, fluke first, then the albies. Until that happens, the smart play is working the rips on the tide changes — Great Point on the ebb, Monomoy's southside on either stage — and staying ready to run to wherever the birds are stacked, because right now that's still the best intel on the water.
